name: Walleye
description: The most prized Great Lakes table fish, with delicate mild-sweet white flesh, a fine moist flake, and a buttery texture best showcased by pan-frying. Fillets contain a central row of pin bones removed by the 'zippering' technique, yielding four boneless portions. Lake Erie wild populations — protected since 1983 gill-net restrictions and Clean Water Act recovery — produce fish of exceptional flavor.
notes: Lean, subtly sweet, low in fishiness — one of the mildest-tasting freshwater fish
Firm yet delicate large flakes hold together well in the pan
Lake Erie is the premier wild fishery; Ohio charter season peaks April–May and September–October
origin: Lake Erie, centered in Ohio waters — the lake produces more walleye than all other Great Lakes combined, its cold, turbid shallows and hard gravel bottoms sustaining wild populations without stocking.

name: Yellow Perch
description: Small but intensely flavorful — the fish fry staple across Great Lakes communities. Lake Erie yields exceptional perch. Restaurants throughout the region feature Friday perch dinners year-round.
notes: Sweet, delicate white flesh with pronounced fresh lake flavor
origin: Lake Erie (finest quality, especially Ohio nearshore), Lake Michigan (Green Bay), Lake Huron — inshore and nearshore structure

name: Chinook Salmon
description: The largest Pacific salmon, transplanted to the Great Lakes in the 1960s to control alewife populations. Now a massive sport fishery. Fall run fish enter tributary rivers — Lake Michigan tributaries are legendary for this.
notes: Rich, fatty, deeply flavorful with vivid orange-red flesh
origin: Lake Michigan (offshore May–August; Pere Marquette, Platte, Manistee, and St. Joseph rivers in fall), Lake Ontario

name: Coho Salmon
description: Silver-bright and acrobatic, coho salmon run close to shore in spring and push into tributary rivers in early fall. Smaller than Chinook but highly regarded for table quality.
notes: Moderately fatty, bright orange-pink flesh, milder and more delicate than Chinook
origin: Lake Michigan nearshore (spring run), Lake Superior — Bois Brule, Two Harbors tributaries in fall

name: Lake Trout
description: A native cold-water species nearly extirpated by the invasive sea lamprey. Conservation efforts have restored populations in Lake Superior and Lake Huron. Preferred deep, cold water year-round.
notes: Rich, fatty, full-bodied — classic Great Lakes character; excellent smoked
origin: Lake Superior (strongest restored native population — Apostle Islands, Pictured Rocks), Lake Huron (Drummond Island area) — deepwater 100–300 ft

name: Brown Trout
description: Originally from Europe, brown trout now thrive in cold, clear Great Lakes tributaries and nearshore areas. Fall spawning runs bring large fish into rivers — a dramatic sight in midwest streams.
notes: Mild to moderately rich, fine-flaked, clean tasting
origin: Lake Michigan nearshore (Milwaukee to Waukegan corridor), cold-water tributaries — Au Sable, Manistee, Pigeon rivers (Michigan); Root and Milwaukee rivers (Wisconsin)

name: Steelhead Trout
description: The Great Lakes strain of rainbow trout that migrates into rivers to spawn. A powerful, acrobatic fish beloved by fly anglers. Spring runs up midwest rivers — the St. Joseph, Platte, and Muskegon — are renowned.
notes: Mild to moderately rich, pink-orange flesh, clean and delicate
origin: Lake Michigan tributaries (Muskegon, Platte, St. Joseph, Betsie rivers — Michigan), Lake Superior (Brule River, Wisconsin)

name: Lake Whitefish
description: A beloved native Great Lakes species with buttery, rich white flesh. Famous throughout the upper midwest in smoked form. Fat content peaks in late fall and winter, making this the ideal harvest season.
notes: Rich, buttery, mild — exceptional smoked; the best freshwater fish for smoking
origin: Lake Superior (commercial fishery centered on Bayfield, Wisconsin and Keweenaw Bay, Michigan), Lake Michigan (Naubinway, Michigan), Lake Huron — deepwater 60–200 ft

name: Northern Pike
description: A formidable ambush predator found throughout Great Lakes tributary marshes and bays. Notorious for Y-shaped bones, but larger fish over 5 lbs have proportionally fewer bones and are more practical table fish.
notes: Mild, white, very clean — excellent when prepared fresh
origin: Green Bay (Lake Michigan), Saginaw Bay (Lake Huron), western Lake Erie marshes — also inland lakes throughout Wisconsin, Michigan, and Minnesota

name: Smallmouth Bass
description: One of North America's most prized sport fish — powerful, fast, and acrobatic. Found in clear rocky Great Lakes shallows. Mostly catch-and-release, but legal to keep in season. Size limit regulations protect the fishery.
notes: Mild, clean, white flesh
origin: Lake Erie (south bass Island, Kelleys Island rocky reefs), Lake Ontario, Lake Huron rocky shorelines; St. Clair River; gravel-bottomed rivers throughout the Ozarks and Great Lakes basin

name: Asparagus
description: Slender, tender shoots with a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor best showcased by simple preparations—grilled, roasted, or sautéed briefly in olive oil. Thin spears are ideal for quick cooking (2–4 minutes); thicker spears suit grilling and roasting at 400°F. Local Michigan and Illinois asparagus from direct farm suppliers reaches Chicago markets in April and May, weeks fresher and more tender than off-season imports.
notes: Snap off the woody base by bending gently until the stalk breaks naturally—no knife needed.
Nichols Farm & Orchard offers weekly CSA pickups at multiple Chicago neighborhood locations including Lincoln Park, West Loop, South Loop, and Logan Square.
Peak season is mid-April through May; early April and June supplies are more limited and variable depending on spring weather.
origin: Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) supplies Chicago CSA pickups throughout the city, and Spence Farm (Fairbury, IL) distributes from 60+ Central Illinois farms to Chicago chefs and specialty vendors.

name: Rhubarb
description: Brilliant crimson stalks with intense tartness require the leaves to be removed (which contain toxic oxalic acid). Stalks are typically sliced thin (½-inch for pies) or chunky (1-inch for stewing). Best uses are compotes, pies (classically paired with strawberries), and roasting at high heat to concentrate sweetness and develop caramelization. Midwest rhubarb from farm-direct suppliers reaches peak flavor in May and arrives weeks fresher than supermarket imports.
notes: Stew for 5 minutes with water, then cook until thick and clear; roast at high heat for 15–20 minutes until tender and caramelized.

Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) offers CSA pickups at multiple Chicago locations: Lincoln Park, West Loop, South Loop, Logan Square, Andersonville, Uptown, Edgewater, Wicker Park, and Near North.
April through May is peak availability at Chicago CSA and farmers markets; June supply becomes limited and variable depending on weather and demand.
origin: Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) distributes fresh spring rhubarb to Chicago CSA pickups throughout the North Side, West Loop, South Loop, and Logan Square neighborhoods from April through June.

name: Watercress
description: Peppery aquatic greens with a sharp, mustard-like bite best enjoyed raw in salads, sandwiches, and soups, or briefly wilted in hot preparations like stir-fries with garlic. The tender young leaves and thin stems are ideal; remove thick woody stems before cooking. Spring harvests (April–May) are sweetest; summer heat turns watercress bitter and floral. Fall harvests are possible but less reliable. Fresh local watercress from Chicago-area CSAs and farmers markets is noticeably more delicate and flavorful than commodity supermarket imports.
notes: Blanch briefly (1–2 minutes) then ice-shock to retain bright color; sauté quickly in hot oil or butter with garlic to mellow peppery intensity.

Watercress is rarely cultivated commercially in the Midwest—spring availability at Chicago farmers markets (Green City Market, neighborhood CSAs) is seasonal and variable; fall supply is less predictable.
Peak flavor in cool months (March–May, October–November); summer heat above 85°F makes plants bolt and leaves become bitter and unsuitable.
origin: Foraged from cold spring-fed streams or grown at CSA farms throughout the upper Midwest; available seasonally at Chicago farmers markets (Green City Market, neighborhood CSAs) primarily in spring months, though limited commercial Midwest production means availability varies.

name: Green Onions
description: Slender alliums with a crisp white bulb and tender green tops — the white base has a sharp, pungent onion flavor ideal for sautéing and stir-fries, while the mild, grassy green tops work best as a fresh raw garnish or briefly wilted. Essential across Chinese, Korean, and Japanese cuisines. Fresh local green onions keep best for 3–5 days; the tender green tops wilt first.
notes: White bulb adds depth when sautéed or stir-fried in high heat; green tops scatter on top at the end to retain bright color and freshness.
Nichols Farm & Orchard offers weekly CSA pickups at 40+ Chicago-area locations including Lincoln Park, West Loop, and Logan Square.
Peak season May–July; limited availability in April and August depending on spring warmth and early fall weather.
origin: Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) supplies green onions through Chicago CSA pickups; Spence Farm (Fairbury, IL) distributes from Central Illinois farms to Chicago restaurants and specialty vendors.

name: Spinach
description: Tender leaves excel raw in salads or cooked via sautéing, stir-frying, steaming, and creaming; works well in spanakopita, risotto, and soups. Spring spinach is mild and tender; fall spinach — harvested as temperatures cool — is notably sweeter and more flavorful. Fresh local spinach from Chicago CSA suppliers and farmers markets stays crisp 4–5 days refrigerated, far superior in flavor and texture to commodity supermarket imports.
notes: Sauté briefly in olive oil or butter with garlic (1–2 minutes) to retain color and delicate texture; season with lemon juice or acid to brighten flavor.
Nichols Farm & Orchard offers weekly CSA pickups at 40+ Chicago locations including Lincoln Park, West Loop, South Loop, and Logan Square.
Fall spinach (September–November) is sweeter and more robust than spring spinach; peak quality in October after light frosts concentrate sugars.
origin: Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) supplies spinach through Chicago CSA pickups at 40+ neighborhood locations including Lincoln Park, West Loop, and Logan Square; Spence Farm (Fairbury, IL) distributes from 60+ Central Illinois farms to Chicago restaurants.

name: Radishes
description: Spring table radishes (April–May) are tender and mildly peppery; fall radishes (September–October) grow larger and develop deeper, sweeter flavor. Radishes excel raw and thin-sliced in salads, pickles, and open-faced sandwiches; they also roast beautifully with olive oil and lemon at high heat, becoming tender with caramelized edges. Large Asian varieties (daikon, Korean mu) are essential to kimchi, pickling, and stir-fries. Fresh local radishes from Chicago CSA suppliers are crisper and more flavorful than commodity supermarket imports.
notes: Thin-slice raw radishes for salads and garnishes; their peppery bite mellows when cooked—roast at 425°F with oil and salt until tender and caramelized (12–15 minutes).
Nichols Farm & Orchard includes radishes in fall CSA shares with weekly pickups at Lincoln Park, West Loop, South Loop, Logan Square, and other Chicago neighborhoods.
Spring radishes (April–May) bolt and become woody above 70°F; fall planting (August–September) succeeds because cooling temperatures prevent bolting.
Radish greens are fully edible—sauté briefly with garlic or add raw to salads; store greens separately from roots to prevent moisture loss.
origin: Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) supplies radishes year-round through Chicago CSA pickups, with spring and fall varieties from Midwest farms; Asian varieties (daikon, Korean mu) from specialty Asian farms in the Chicago metropolitan area serving Korean and Japanese communities.

name: Garlic Scapes
description: Tender, spiral-shaped shoots harvested from hardneck garlic plants with a mild garlic flavor and crisp-tender texture. Best served grilled with a light char, sautéed with pasta, blended into pesto, or pickled. Blanch briefly (1–2 minutes) then grill or roast at high heat to bring out sweetness. Fresh Chicago-area scapes are crispier and more delicate than commodity imports, with exceptional flavor due to local hardneck garlic cultivation.
notes: Snap off the woody base (similar to asparagus); the tender top 6–8 inches are ideal. Tough bases can be simmered whole in soups like bay leaves.
Froggy Meadow Farm (Beloit, WI, supplying Green City Market Chicago) offers scapes starting mid-June through mid-July at Lincoln Park location.
Harvest window is mid-June in central Midwest; scapes emerge 3–4 weeks before bulb harvest and must be removed to channel energy into bulb development.
origin: Froggy Meadow Farm (Beloit, WI) supplies hardneck garlic scapes exclusively to Green City Market at the Lincoln Park year-round location, with mid-June peak availability; hardneck varieties are the only source of scapes and are rarely found outside farmers markets.

name: Shiso (Perilla)
description: Aromatic Japanese herb with a distinctive anise-basil-mint flavor; green shiso (aojiso) is used fresh as a garnish in sushi, sashimi, salads, and seafood dishes, or fried crisp in tempura (25–30 seconds at 350°F yields best results); red shiso (akajiso) is traditionally used for pickling and seasoning. Fresh local shiso from Chicago-area Japanese farms is noticeably more aromatic and tender than imported specimens.
notes: Aojiso (green) has a sharp, refreshing flavor best enjoyed fresh; akajiso (red) is more astringent and metallic, suited for pickling and colorant.
Tempura frying (25–30 seconds) preserves volatiles better than longer cooking; heat destroys aromatic compounds within 60 seconds except during quick frying.
Hinata Farms (Rachel Kimura, Edgewater/Rogers Park neighborhood) grows shiso and supplies local restaurants; contact rachel@hinatafarms.com or 773.236.7791.
origin: Hinata Farms (Chicago, Edgewater/Rogers Park neighborhood) specializes in Asian heritage vegetables and herbs including shiso and supplies local restaurants and community members.

name: Peas
description: Sugar snap peas and shell peas thrive in cool midwest springs. Snap peas are eaten whole with pods—raw, stir-fried, or briefly roasted at high heat until pods blister; shell peas are shelled and steamed 2–3 minutes or simmered just until tender. Fresh local peas from Chicago CSA suppliers arrive weeks earlier and sweeter than supermarket imports, with a delicate texture that deteriorates rapidly after harvest.
notes: Snap peas: remove string along both seams before eating or cooking; brief high-heat roasting (10 minutes at 450°F) brings out natural sweetness.
Shell peas: steam or simmer 2–3 minutes only—overcooking causes waterlogging and mushy texture; pair with mint, butter, or light cream.
Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) offers weekly CSA pickups at 13+ Chicago locations including Lincoln Park, West Loop, South Loop, Logan Square, and Andersonville starting mid-May.
origin: Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) supplies snap peas and sugar snap peas through weekly Chicago CSA pickups at 13+ neighborhood locations; Spence Farm (Fairbury, IL) distributes from Central Illinois farms to Chicago restaurants and specialty vendors.

name: Bok Choy
description: Tender Chinese cabbage with crisp white stems and mild, slightly sweet flavor—essential to Cantonese and Southeast Asian stir-fries. Baby bok choy (halved lengthwise) and medium bok choy (quartered) cook quickly at high heat in a wok with garlic and oyster sauce in 3–5 minutes; larger varieties require stems and leaves separated, cooked stem-first then leaves added near the end. Fresh local bok choy from Chicago-area Asian farms stays crisp 4–5 days refrigerated, superior in texture and flavor to year-round commodity imports.
notes: High-heat wok cooking (2–3 minutes for baby bok choy halved, 1–2 minutes for leaves alone) preserves tender-crisp texture; blanch then pan-sear for a restaurant-style seared edge.
Urban Growers Collective (Chicago CSA) and Chicago Botanic Garden offer bok choy through seasonal produce boxes and weekly CSA pickups.
Peak season May–June (spring crop) and September–October (fall crop); bok choy dislikes heat above 70°F so summer availability is limited and may come from imports.
origin: Hinata Farms and Asian specialty farms serving Chicago's Edgewater, Rogers Park, and western suburban Chinese and Korean communities; available year-round at Asian grocery markets and through CSA programs including Urban Growers Collective and Chicago Botanic Garden.

name: Kohlrabi
description: Mild-flavored bulb with a texture between broccoli stem and apple—best raw in slaws and sliced thin on a mandoline, roasted at 400°F until caramelized (25 min), or sautéed whole and peeled. The tender young greens are fully edible, treated like other crucifer greens. Fresh local kohlrabi from Chicago CSA suppliers is crisper and more delicate than supermarket imports, with superior flavor in spring and fall harvests when cool weather prevents bolting.
notes: Remove the tough outer skin with a vegetable peeler before cooking or eating raw.
Roast at 400°F with olive oil and salt 20–25 minutes until tender and caramelized; the interior sweetens dramatically with heat.
Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) includes kohlrabi in seasonal CSA shares with weekly pickups at 40+ Chicago neighborhoods; Spence Farm (Fairbury, IL) supplies restaurants and specialty vendors.
A cold-season crop: spring kohlrabi (April–May) bolts above 70°F; fall crop (August–September planting) succeeds because cooling weather prevents premature bolting.
origin: Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) supplies kohlrabi through Chicago CSA pickups and Green City Market; Spence Farm (Fairbury, IL) grows kohlrabi and distributes from Central Illinois farms to Chicago restaurants and specialty vendors.

name: Strawberries
description: Intensely fragrant and sweet, midwest strawberries peak in early June and are far superior to off-season imports. Their season is brief — the flavor deteriorates within days of picking.
notes: High in vitamin C
Rich in antioxidants
Good source of fiber
origin: Michigan (Ottawa, Van Buren, and Berrien counties), Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois; u-pick farms throughout the Midwest are the primary retail source

name: Sweet Cherries
description: Dark, juicy sweet cherries ripen in mid-July across Michigan orchards. A brief, precious season — best eaten within days of picking.
notes: Anti-inflammatory compounds
Natural melatonin source
Rich in antioxidants
origin: Michigan — Leelanau and Grand Traverse counties (the Old Mission and Leelanau peninsulas produce nearly 80% of U.S. sweet cherries some years)

name: Tart Cherries
description: Michigan is the nation's top producer of Montmorency tart cherries. These brilliant red, intensely flavored cherries are ideal for preserves, pies, and juice.
notes: High in anti-inflammatory compounds
Rich in melatonin
Good source of vitamins A and C
origin: Michigan — Traverse City region (Grand Traverse, Benzie, and Antrim counties) produces roughly 75% of the U.S. tart cherry crop; Montmorency is the dominant variety

name: Blueberries
description: Plump, dusty-blue berries cluster on low bushes across the upper midwest. Michigan ranks among the top producing states in the nation.
notes: Highest antioxidant content of any common fruit
Brain health benefits
Rich in vitamins C and K
origin: Michigan — Van Buren and Allegan counties (southwestern) and Oceana County lead state production; also northern Michigan near Muskegon and Newaygo counties

name: Raspberries
description: Delicate ruby-red raspberries require careful picking but reward with intense flavor. Some farms have a fall second crop in September.
notes: High in fiber
Rich in antioxidants
Good source of vitamins C and K
origin: Michigan (Ottawa and Kent counties), Minnesota, and Wisconsin; u-pick farms throughout the upper Midwest; Minnesota is a leading state for bramble fruit production

name: Plums
description: Juicy stone fruit with a tart skin and sweet flesh. Both Japanese and European varieties grow in midwest orchards, offering a long combined season from July through September.
notes: Good source of vitamins C and K
Contains sorbitol (digestive aid)
Rich in antioxidants
origin: Michigan (Berrien and Van Buren counties), Ohio, and Indiana; Italian prune plums common in Wisconsin orchards with German-heritage roots; Japanese varieties from Michigan and Illinois

name: Cantaloupe
description: Sweet, fragrant muskmelons grown across the midwest, with heavy production in Illinois and Indiana. The best ones smell like perfume through a paper bag.
notes: Rich in beta-carotene
High in vitamin C and potassium
Very high water content (hydrating)
origin: Indiana (especially the southwestern counties along the Wabash River) and Illinois (Henderson and Knox counties); roadside stands in central Indiana are a regional landmark

name: Watermelon
description: Juicy, sweet melons grown across the midwest, especially in Indiana and Illinois. Summer heat is essential for developing the high sugar content midwest watermelons are known for.
notes: 92% water (hydrating)
Rich in lycopene
Good source of vitamins A and C
origin: Indiana (Rush and Shelby counties lead state production) and Illinois; Missouri is a significant producer; roadside farm stands are the primary retail channel

name: Peaches
description: Fragrant, dripping-ripe midwest peaches are a fleeting late-summer treasure. Michigan's southwestern counties produce some of the finest peaches in the country.
notes: Good source of vitamins C and A
Rich in potassium
High in fiber
origin: Michigan — Berrien, Van Buren, and Allegan counties (the Lake Michigan fruit belt, where the lake moderates temperature); also southern Illinois and Indiana

name: Zucchini
description: Tender young zucchini excel when cooked quickly at high heat—grilling, roasting at 400–450°F, or brief sautéing—to prevent waterlogging. Remove the soft seed core before cooking by halving lengthwise, then cut into spears or rounds. Fresh local zucchini from Chicago CSA suppliers arrives weeks fresher than commodity supermarket imports, with superior delicate flavor and firm texture.
notes: Roast at high heat (400–450°F) with ample space between pieces; avoid salting before cooking as it draws moisture and causes mushiness.
Grill or sauté zucchini spears quickly (3–5 minutes) with olive oil at high heat to caramelize edges and concentrate flavor.

Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) offers zucchini through weekly Chicago CSA pickups at 40+ locations including Lincoln Park, West Loop, South Loop, Logan Square, and other neighborhoods June–September.
origin: Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) supplies fresh zucchini through Chicago CSA pickups at 40+ neighborhood locations including Lincoln Park, West Loop, South Loop, and Logan Square; available June through September.

name: Thai Basil
description: Aromatic Southeast Asian herb with distinctive anise-clove flavor essential to Thai, Lao, Cambodian, and Vietnamese cooking. Use fresh in stir-fries (pad krapow gai), fried rice, and curries — add at the end of cooking to preserve volatile aromatics and bright green color. The sturdy leaves withstand high heat better than Italian basil. Fresh local Thai basil from Chicago-area farms is noticeably more aromatic and tender than dried imports or year-round supermarket specimens.
notes: Add Thai basil in the final 30 seconds of high-heat stir-frying; turn off heat and stir until just wilted to retain color and anise flavor.
Hinata Farms (Chicago, Edgewater/Rogers Park) specializes in Asian heritage herbs and supplies local restaurants; contact rachel@hinatafarms.com or 773.236.7791.
Thai basil is a warm-season crop requiring full sun; peak supply in Chicago is July–August when summer heat maximizes leaf flavor and plant vigor.
origin: Hinata Farms (Chicago, Edgewater/Rogers Park neighborhood) grows Asian herbs including Thai basil and supplies local restaurants and community members; contact rachel@hinatafarms.com or 773.236.7791.

name: Cucumbers
description: Cool, crisp summer vegetable with thin, tender skins ideal for pickling and fresh eating. Japanese and Korean thin-skin varieties excel in quick pickles, oi muchim (Korean cucumber salad), and Japanese namasu. Slice thinly for Japanese preparations or halve lengthwise for pickling; high-heat pickling vinegar (5% acidity) yields the crispest texture. Fresh local cucumbers from Chicago CSA suppliers stay crisp 5–7 days refrigerated, far superior in flavor and texture to commodity supermarket imports.
notes: Japanese thin-skin cucumbers (virtually seedless, mild flavor) are ideal for quick pickles and fresh preparations; Korean varieties are equally suited for fermented oiji and spicy oi muchim.
Hinata Farms (Chicago, Edgewater/Rogers Park) specializes in Japanese heritage vegetables including thin-skin cucumber varieties; contact rachel@hinatafarms.com or 773.236.7791.
Peak season July–August in Chicago; Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) offers cucumbers through weekly CSA pickups at 40+ Chicago locations June–September.
origin: Hinata Farms (Chicago, Edgewater/Rogers Park) grows Japanese thin-skin cucumber varieties and supplies local restaurants; also available through Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) CSA pickups and Chicago farmers markets.

name: Cherry Tomatoes
description: Small, intensely sweet tomatoes prized for roasting at high heat (400–425°F for 18–30 minutes) until skins blister and interiors turn jammy, concentrating natural sugars into a quick sauce for pasta. Raw in salads, or halved and blistered in a dry pan with garlic and oil. Fresh local cherry tomatoes from Chicago CSA suppliers arrive weeks fresher than commodity supermarket imports, with superior sweetness and firm skin texture.
notes: Roast halved cherry tomatoes at 400–425°F for 18–30 minutes with olive oil, garlic, and herbs to concentrate flavor and create a ready-made sauce.
Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) offers cherry tomatoes through weekly Chicago CSA pickups at 40+ locations July–October.
Cherry tomatoes ripen 2–3 weeks before large-fruited heirloom and paste varieties, making them the most reliable fresh tomato for continuous summer harvest through early fall.
origin: Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) supplies fresh cherry tomatoes through Chicago CSA pickups at 40+ neighborhood locations including Lincoln Park, West Loop, South Loop, and Logan Square; also available at farmers markets throughout the region.

name: Heirloom Tomatoes
description: Open-pollinated varieties with complex, deep flavor—colors range from deep purple (Cherokee Purple) to striped green to bright yellow (Brandywine). Best served raw and sliced thick (½ to ¾ inch) in salads with minimal dressing (olive oil, vinegar, salt, fresh basil); the natural juices concentrate flavor when tomatoes rest for 15–20 minutes. Heirloom tomatoes from Chicago-area CSAs and local farmers arrive weeks fresher than commodity imports, with superior acidity balance and aromatic volatiles that deteriorate rapidly after harvest.
notes: Slice with a serrated knife to avoid crushing; allow 15–20 minutes of resting time for juices to concentrate and natural sugars to develop.
Serve at room temperature with sea salt, olive oil, and acid (vinegar or lemon juice); fresh basil, onion, and herbs complete the dish.
Nichols Farm & Orchard offers heirloom tomatoes through CSA pickups and Green City Market (Lincoln Park winter location, Saturdays 8 am–1 pm).
Peak season late July through September; August is prime availability at Chicago farmers markets.
origin: Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) supplies heirloom tomatoes through Chicago CSA pickups at 40+ neighborhood locations including Lincoln Park, West Loop, South Loop, and Logan Square; Jon Templin of Butternut Sustainable Farms (Sturgis, MI) grows 30+ heirloom varieties and supplies top Chicago restaurants; Chicago Tomato Man (Bob Zeni, LaGrange Park) offers 120+ heirloom seedling varieties through pop-up sales throughout Chicago.

name: Roma / Paste Tomatoes
description: Thick-walled, low-moisture paste tomatoes ideal for sauce, canning, and paste-making. Their meaty flesh, few seeds, and dense interior concentrate flavor under low-heat simmering (2–3 hours) or high-heat roasting (30–40 minutes at 375°F) to develop jammy sweetness and umami depth. Fresh Chicago-area roma tomatoes from local CSAs arrive weeks fresher and firmer than commodity supermarket imports, making them superior for both fresh preparations and preservation.
notes: Simmer slowly (2–3 hours) with olive oil and herbs to concentrate flavor and create thick, rich sauce; high-heat roasting develops caramelized, concentrated sweetness.

Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) supplies fresh roma tomatoes through Chicago CSA pickups at 40+ neighborhood locations including Lincoln Park, West Loop, South Loop, and Logan Square from August through October.
Peak availability September at Chicago farmers markets and CSA pickups; August and October supplies are variable and depend on summer heat and early fall weather.
origin: Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) supplies fresh roma tomatoes through Chicago CSA pickups at 40+ neighborhood locations including Lincoln Park, West Loop, South Loop, and Logan Square; Spence Farm (Fairbury, IL) distributes from Central Illinois farms to Chicago restaurants and specialty vendors.

name: Eggplant
description: Japanese and Chinese eggplant varieties thrive in midwest summer heat — slender, thin-skinned, sweeter and less bitter than globe eggplant. Japanese eggplant excels grilled, sautéed, or pan-fried briefly (4–6 minutes) until skin blisters and flesh turns silky and melt-in-mouth; Chinese eggplant suits longer stir-fries, braises, and stews where the tender skin adds flavor and visual appeal. Unlike globe eggplant, Asian varieties rarely require salting. Fresh local eggplant from Chicago-area farms is firmer and more flavorful than commodity supermarket imports.
notes: Japanese eggplant (finger-length, deep purple) cooks rapidly at high heat with minimal pre-treatment; do not salt before cooking as Asian varieties lack the bitterness of globe types.
Hinata Farms (Chicago, Edgewater/Rogers Park) grows Japanese eggplant and supplies local restaurants; contact rachel@hinatafarms.com or 773.236.7791.
Peak supply July–September in Chicago; early July and late September availability is limited and variable depending on summer heat and early fall temperatures.
origin: Hinata Farms (Chicago, Edgewater/Rogers Park neighborhood) grows Japanese eggplant varieties and supplies local restaurants; also available through Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) CSA pickups and Chicago farmers markets.

name: Sweet Corn
description: Peak-season sweet corn harvested within hours of use is incomparably sweeter and more tender than commodity supermarket imports. Boil 3–7 minutes depending on ear size (never salt the water), grill 10–15 minutes with husks on for smoky char, or steam 4–6 minutes to preserve nutrients. Also excellent in soups, chowders, fritters, and creamed corn. Fresh local corn from Chicago CSA suppliers arrives weeks fresher than off-season imports, with superior natural sweetness and tender kernel texture.
notes: Boil or steam just 3–7 minutes to retain sweetness and tender texture; overcooking causes starch conversion and mushy kernels.
Grill with husks intact 10–15 minutes, turning occasionally, for caramelized char and smoky flavor while kernels remain tender inside.
Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) offers fresh sweet corn through weekly Chicago CSA pickups at 40+ locations July–September; peak availability in August.
Corn sweetness peaks at harvest and deteriorates within hours—select ears with moist green husks and kernels that puncture easily to release milky liquid.
origin: Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) supplies fresh sweet corn through Chicago CSA pickups at 40+ neighborhood locations including Lincoln Park, West Loop, South Loop, and Logan Square; also available at Chicago farmers markets including Green City Market and Daley Plaza.

name: Green Beans
description: Tender snap beans excel blanched 2–3 minutes then shocked in ice water to retain crispness, sautéed briefly in butter or olive oil, or stir-fried at high heat. Yard-long beans (18–24 inches, preferred for Asian cooking) wok-fry with oyster sauce and ginger in 5–8 minutes. Fresh local green beans from Chicago CSA suppliers arrive weeks fresher and crisper than commodity supermarket imports, retaining delicate flavor and vibrant color.
notes: Blanch 2–3 minutes at rolling boil, then shock in ice water to halt cooking and set bright green color; drain well before finishing preparations.
Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) includes green beans in weekly CSA pickups at 40+ Chicago locations including Lincoln Park, West Loop, South Loop, and Logan Square.
Yard-long beans (chewy, sturdy texture suited to intense spices) require 5–8 minutes high-heat stir-frying; standard snap beans cook faster (3–5 minutes sautéed or steamed).
Peak supply July–August in Chicago; early July and September availability is variable depending on planting schedules and early fall weather.
origin: Nichols Farm & Orchard (Marengo, IL) supplies green beans through Chicago CSA pickups at 40+ neighborhood locations; yard-long beans (preferred for Asian stir-fries) from specialty Asian farms in the Chicago area.

name: Garlic
description: Fresh-harvested garlic in summer has a sweeter, more complex flavor than cured storage garlic. Hardneck varieties (Rocambole, Porcelain) are preferred by chefs for their nuanced heat.
notes: Allicin for immune support
Anti-inflammatory
Cardiovascular benefits
origin: Small-farm production throughout the upper Midwest — Wisconsin (Driftless Area), northern Michigan, and Minnesota; Music and German Red (hardneck Porcelain/Rocambole) are leading regional varieties

name: Peppers
description: Sweet bells and hot chili varieties ripen through late summer into fall. Korean varieties (cheongyang, gochugaru types) grow well in midwest heat.
notes: Extremely high in vitamin C (red > green)
Capsaicin metabolic boost
Rich in antioxidants
origin: Michigan (leading bell pepper state in the Midwest), Ohio, and Indiana; Korean hot pepper varieties from specialty Asian community farms in Chicago, Detroit, and Columbus

name: Edamame
description: Fresh soybeans in the fuzzy green pod, grown throughout midwest farm country. The flavor difference between fresh and frozen edamame is dramatic — fresh is sweet and grassy.
notes: Complete plant protein
High in folate
Rich in iron and calcium
origin: Illinois (the nation's top soybean state), Iowa, and Indiana; fresh edamame varieties (distinct from field corn soybeans) grown at Japanese and Korean community farms in Chicago and Detroit metro areas

name: Shishito Peppers
description: Thin-skinned, mildly hot Japanese peppers that blister beautifully in a dry cast iron pan. About one in ten is surprisingly spicy — part of the Russian roulette appeal.
notes: Good source of vitamins A and C
Low calorie
Antioxidant-rich
origin: Japanese-variety specialty farms in the Chicago, Detroit, and Columbus metro areas; increasingly grown at mainstream CSA farms throughout the Midwest as demand from Japanese and Korean restaurants has grown

name: Beets
description: Earthy and sweet, beets are harvested from early summer through fall. The greens are also edible — don't throw them away. Yellow and chioggia varieties each have distinct, milder flavors.
notes: High in folate
Rich in nitrates for blood pressure
Good source of manganese
origin: Wisconsin and Michigan lead Midwest beet production; sugar beet farming is historically significant in Michigan's Thumb region (Saginaw Valley) and Minnesota's Red River Valley

name: Tomatillos
description: Tart, citrusy fruits in papery husks. A warm-season crop that thrives in midwest summer heat. Grown at many midwest farms, especially those serving Latin communities.
notes: Good source of vitamin C
Contains potassium
Low calorie
origin: Illinois (Chicago metropolitan area, serving large Mexican-American community), Indiana, and Ohio; small-farm production at Latino-run CSA farms; widely available at Mexican grocers sourced from regional farms

name: Fennel
description: Anise-flavored vegetable with a crisp white bulb and feathery green fronds. Less common at midwest markets but available at farms catering to diverse clientele.
notes: Good source of vitamin C and fiber
Contains anethole (anti-inflammatory)
Rich in potassium
origin: Specialty produce farms throughout the Midwest; Italian-heritage communities in Chicago (especially the Western suburbs) and Cleveland maintain local demand; available at CSA farms and co-ops

name: Napa Cabbage
description: The essential kimchi ingredient — grows abundantly in cool fall weather. Heads become sweet and crisp after light frosts. A pillar of Korean autumn food culture.
notes: Very low calorie
Rich in vitamins C and K
Contains folate and potassium
origin: Asian specialty farms in the Chicago, Detroit, Columbus, and Minneapolis metro areas; Korean-American community farms in the Chicago suburbs (especially Glenview and Naperville corridors) are primary producers

name: Daikon
description: Large white radishes with mild sweetness and crunch. A cornerstone of Japanese and Korean cooking. Grows to impressive size in cool midwest fall soil.
notes: Contains digestive enzymes
Low calorie
Good source of vitamin C
origin: Japanese and Korean specialty farms in the Midwest; significant production at farms serving Chicago's Japantown (Edgewater/Rogers Park) and Korean-American communities in the western suburbs; also Twin Cities area

name: Kabocha Squash
description: Japanese pumpkin with dense, sweet, chestnut-flavored flesh and a dry texture. Dark green skin, vibrantly orange inside. Grows well in midwest gardens.
notes: Very high in beta-carotene
Rich in vitamins A and C
Good source of iron
origin: Japanese specialty farms throughout the Midwest; commonly grown at farms in Michigan, Wisconsin, and Ohio serving Japanese and Korean communities; increasingly available at mainstream farmers markets

name: Butternut Squash
description: Nutty, sweet winter squash with tan skin and bright orange flesh. A prolific midwest fall crop that stores well through winter.
notes: High in beta-carotene
Good source of vitamins C and E
Rich in potassium
origin: Grown across the Midwest; Michigan, Ohio, and Illinois lead regional production; roadside stands and pumpkin farms throughout Indiana and Illinois are the primary retail source

name: Sweet Potatoes
description: Orange-fleshed roots grown throughout the midwest, especially in Illinois. Require a long warm season — slip planting in May, harvest 90–120 days later.
notes: Very high in beta-carotene (orange types)
Rich in vitamins A and C
Good source of potassium
origin: Illinois (Fulton, Mason, and Tazewell counties along the Illinois River are a historic sweet potato belt), Indiana, and Missouri; Jewel and Beauregard are the dominant midwest varieties

name: Leeks
description: Mild, sweet alliums with a long white shaft and dark green tops. More delicate than onions. Grow well in midwest conditions and improve with cool fall weather.
notes: Rich in vitamin K
Good source of folate
Contains prebiotic fiber
origin: Specialty produce farms in Wisconsin, Michigan, and Minnesota; European-heritage farm communities in Wisconsin (particularly Belgian and Dutch communities in Kewaunee and Door counties) have a long leek-growing tradition

name: Asian Pears
description: Crisp, apple-shaped pears with delicate floral sweetness. Unlike European pears, they are ripe when still firm. Grown in select midwest orchards.
notes: High in fiber
Good source of vitamin C
Rich in copper
origin: Specialty orchards in Michigan (Berrien and Van Buren counties) and Ohio; Korean-American farm operations in the Chicago and Columbus metro areas; supplemented by Pacific Northwest imports at Asian markets

name: European Pears
description: Classic European pears ripen off the tree, sweetening as they soften. Bartlett, Bosc, and Anjou varieties are all grown in midwest orchards. U-pick pear farms are less common than apples.
notes: High in fiber
Good source of vitamin C
Contains copper
origin: Michigan (Berrien and Van Buren counties, within the Lake Michigan fruit belt), Ohio, and Wisconsin; Bartlett is the most common Midwest variety; smaller volumes than apple or cherry production

name: Apples — Early Season
description: The first apples of the season arrive in July and August. Varieties like Paula Red and Zestar are crisp, sweet, and a welcome sign of the upcoming fall harvest.
notes: Rich in quercetin
High in soluble fiber (pectin)
Good source of vitamin C
origin: Michigan (the nation's third-largest apple state — Oceana, Kent, and Ionia counties); Wisconsin (Door County); Paula Red is a Michigan-originated variety (Sparta, Kent County)

name: Apples — Honeycrisp & Midseason
description: The peak of apple season. Honeycrisp's legendary crunch and balanced sweetness made it a phenomenon — it was developed at the University of Minnesota and thrives in midwest conditions.
notes: Rich in quercetin
High in soluble fiber (pectin)
Good source of vitamin C
origin: Developed at the University of Minnesota Horticultural Research Center (Excelsior, MN) and released in 1991; primary production in Michigan (Oceana, Ionia, Kent counties), Minnesota, and Wisconsin (Door County)

name: Apples — Late Season
description: The final apple varieties of the season bring deep flavor and excellent storage qualities. Late-season apples like Fuji and Empire can be cellared through winter.
notes: Rich in quercetin
High in soluble fiber (pectin)
Good source of vitamin C
origin: Michigan (Oceana, Kent, and Ionia counties remain primary); Fuji is of Japanese origin but now widely grown in Michigan; Empire developed at Cornell but flourishes in both Michigan and Wisconsin orchards

name: Grapes
description: Concord, Niagara, and wine grape varieties ripen across midwest vineyards in September. The Concord grape's distinctive 'foxy' aroma is uniquely American.
notes: Rich in resveratrol
High in antioxidants
Good source of vitamins C and K
origin: Michigan (Fennville and the Lake Michigan Shore AVA), Ohio (Lake Erie shore — Sandusky to Conneaut), Indiana (Lake Michigan shore, Chesterton area); Concord originated in Concord, Massachusetts but the Great Lakes shore became its heartland

name: Wild Mushrooms
description: The midwest's deciduous forests yield exceptional wild mushroom harvests. Morel hunting is a beloved spring tradition; fall brings maitake, chanterelles, and oyster mushrooms.
notes: Natural vitamin D source
Rich in B vitamins
Immune-supporting beta-glucans
origin: Foraged throughout Midwest deciduous forests — morels peak in May in southern Michigan and Indiana; maitake and hen-of-the-woods from oak forests in southern Wisconsin, Illinois, and Indiana; chanterelles in northern Michigan and Minnesota mixed forests

name: Kale
description: Cold-hardy kale is one of the few vegetables available into midwest winter. Frost-sweetened October and November kale is far better than summer kale.
notes: Extremely high in vitamins K and A
Rich in iron
High in antioxidants
origin: Grown across the Midwest at market farms and CSAs; Michigan and Wisconsin lead regional production; hoop-house and tunnel farming extends the season well into December in the upper Midwest

name: Gai Lan
description: Chinese broccoli (芥蘭) with glossy leaves and thick stems. A pillar of Cantonese cooking with a pleasantly bitter flavor, deeper than regular broccoli. Widely available at Asian grocery stores.
notes: Very high in vitamins C and K
Rich in calcium
Contains beta-carotene
origin: Specialty Asian produce farms in the Chicago, Detroit, and Columbus metro areas; Cantonese community farms in the Chicago western suburbs and Michigan's Ann Arbor area are primary producers; widely supplemented by California imports at Asian grocers

name: Yu Choy
description: Tender Chinese flowering greens (油菜心) with small yellow flowers and smooth stems. One of the most popular vegetables in Cantonese cooking — mild, slightly sweet, with delicate texture.
notes: High in vitamins C and K
Good source of folate
Rich in calcium
origin: Asian specialty farms in the Chicago, Detroit, and Columbus metro areas; Cantonese community farmers in the Chicago western suburbs; California and Florida imports fill gaps at Asian grocery stores

name: Bitter Melon
description: Intensely bitter, distinctively wrinkled green gourd (苦瓜) essential to Chinese, Korean, and Southeast Asian cooking. Grows well in midwest summer heat. An acquired taste with devoted fans.
notes: Contains charantin (blood sugar regulation)
Rich in vitamin C
Anti-inflammatory
origin: Chinese and Southeast Asian specialty farms in the Chicago, Detroit, and Columbus areas; Hmong farmers in the Minneapolis–St. Paul area are major producers; supplemented year-round by Florida and California imports at Asian markets

name: Garlic Chives
description: Flat-leaved Chinese chives (韭菜) with a garlic-onion flavor more assertive than Western chives. A cornerstone of Chinese and Korean cooking. The flower buds in late summer are a seasonal delicacy.
notes: Rich in vitamins A and C
Contains flavonoids
Digestive benefits
origin: Chinese and Korean specialty farms throughout the Midwest; widely grown at community garden plots and small-farm operations serving Asian-American communities in Chicago, Detroit, Columbus, and the Twin Cities

name: Water Spinach
description: Hollow-stemmed aquatic greens (空心菜) essential to Chinese, Thai, and Filipino cooking. The distinctive hollow stems give a unique tender-crisp texture when stir-fried at high heat.
notes: Rich in vitamins A and C
High in iron
Good source of calcium
origin: Southeast Asian and Chinese specialty farms in the Midwest — Hmong farmers in the Minneapolis–St. Paul and Milwaukee areas are among the primary producers; also Chinese-run farms in the Chicago and Detroit metro areas

name: Chrysanthemum Greens
description: Fragrant, slightly bitter greens (茼蒿) with a distinctive herby-floral flavor. Related to the ornamental chrysanthemum but bred for culinary use. A classic hot pot and nabe vegetable.
notes: Rich in vitamins A and C
Contains luteolin (anti-inflammatory)
High in minerals
origin: Japanese and Chinese specialty farms in the Midwest; available at Asian grocery stores throughout the region; commonly grown at Nikkei community garden plots in Chicago (Edgewater) and Detroit (Islandview)

name: Chinese Mustard Greens
description: Pungent, peppery greens (芥菜) with broad leaves and thick stems. A staple of Cantonese and Sichuan cooking. Both fresh and pickled forms are widely important in Chinese cuisine.
notes: Excellent source of vitamins C and K
Anti-inflammatory glucosinolates
High in calcium
origin: Cantonese and Sichuan community farms in the Chicago, Detroit, and Columbus metro areas; also grown by Hmong farmers in the Twin Cities; supplemented by California and Florida imports at Chinese and Vietnamese grocery stores

name: Luffa
description: Tender Asian gourd (丝瓜) with mild, slightly sweet flavor and silky texture. Completely different from the mature dried loofah sponge. A beloved summer vegetable in Chinese cooking.
notes: Low calorie
Good source of vitamin C
Contains anti-inflammatory compounds
origin: Chinese specialty farms in the Chicago, Detroit, and Columbus metro areas; grown at community gardens serving Chinese and Vietnamese populations; requires a long warm season so Midwest production is centered in Indiana, Illinois, and southern Ohio
